title: Why You'd Never Want to Meet a Neutron Star
screen_title: Why You'd Never Want to Meet a Neutron Star
subtitle: The strangest objects in the universe
yt_title: Why You'd Never Want to Meet a Neutron Star
intro: A neutron star is the crushed heart of a dead star: heavier than the Sun, smaller than a city, spinning hundreds of times a second. We fly to one and find out what its gravity, its radiation and its magnetic field would do to you, visit the pulsars and magnetars, and see how colliding neutron stars made the gold in your jewelry.
questions: Did you know a teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tons?
Would you rather visit a pulsar or a magnetar, from a very safe distance?
What should we never get close to next?

segments.text: Somewhere in our galaxy, there's an object heavier than the Sun, squeezed into a ball smaller than a city. It spins hundreds of times a second. And if you got close, it would flatten you thinner than a sheet of paper.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: neutron star illustration

segments.text: Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we visit a neutron star, and find out why you'd never want to meet one.

visual.query: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way)

segments.chapter: How a neutron star is born
segments.text: To understand a neutron star, we have to watch a giant star die. Stars much heavier than our Sun burn their fuel fast, in just a few million years.

files: Grand star-forming region R136 in NGC 2070 (captured by the Hubble Space Telescope).jpg
visual.query: Grand star-forming region R136 in NGC 2070 (captured by the Hubble Space Telescope)

segments.headline: A giant star

segments.text: When the fuel runs out, the core can no longer hold itself up against its own weight. In less than a second, it collapses.

files: New Hubble Observations of Supernova 1987A Trace Shock Wave (4954621859).jpg
visual.query: New Hubble Observations of Supernova 1987A Trace Shock Wave (4954621859)

segments.headline: Collapse

segments.text: The outer layers blast away in a supernova, one of the brightest explosions in the universe. For a few weeks, a single dying star can outshine its whole galaxy.

files: Keplers supernova.jpg
visual.query: Keplers supernova

segments.headline: Supernova

segments.text: In the year ten fifty-four, astronomers in China recorded a new star so bright it was visible in daylight for weeks. Today we can still see the wreckage: the Crab Nebula.

files: Crab Nebula.jpg
visual.query: Crab Nebula

segments.headline: The Crab Nebula

segments.text: And right in its center, there's what was left behind: a neutron star, still spinning, still glowing.

files: Moving heart of the Crab Nebula.jpg
visual.query: Moving heart of the Crab Nebula

segments.text: So what is a neutron star? Imagine squeezing a star so hard that its atoms are crushed. Electrons are pushed into protons, and they turn into neutrons.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron)

segments.headline: Crushed atoms

segments.text: The result is a ball only about twenty kilometers wide. About the size of a city.

visual.label: wide
visual.sub: about the size of a city

segments.text: But it weighs more than our Sun. Usually about one and a half times as much.
A single teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons. More than every car on Earth put together.
Here's my first question. Did you know a single teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tons? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Did you know a teaspoon of a neutron star weighs about a billion tons?

segments.text: Now let's fly closer. The nearest known neutron stars are hundreds of light-years away. That's a good thing.

files: Guisard - Milky Way.jpg
visual.query: Guisard - Milky Way

segments.headline: Hundreds of light-years away

segments.text: From a distance, you'd see a tiny, brilliant point, glowing in X-rays. Its surface can be around a million degrees Celsius.

files: Chandra X-ray Observations of the Crab Nebula (2011-crab-more-2 - 154).jpg
visual.query: Chandra X-ray Observations of the Crab Nebula (2011-crab-more-2 - 154)

segments.headline: Glowing in X-rays

segments.text: As you approach, the first danger is radiation. Many neutron stars blast out X-rays and gamma rays, enough to kill an unprotected astronaut long before arrival.

files: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept.jpg
visual.query: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept

segments.headline: Radiation

segments.text: Then there's the gravity. The pull is so strong that it bends light around the star. From close by, you could see part of its back side.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron)

segments.headline: Light bends

segments.text: At the surface, gravity is about two hundred billion times stronger than on Earth.
Drop something from just one meter high, and it would hit the ground at about two thousand kilometers per second. More than seven million kilometers an hour.
And long before you reached the surface, the difference in pull between your feet and your head would stretch you apart. Then you'd be flattened into a layer thinner than a sheet of paper.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron)

segments.headline: Flattened

segments.text: Its surface is the smoothest thing we know. The tallest mountains are thought to be less than a millimeter high. Gravity pulls everything flat.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron)

segments.headline: The smoothest ball

segments.text: So what's inside? Nobody has ever seen. But physicists have some amazing ideas.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron)

segments.headline: What's inside?

segments.text: The outer crust is thought to be a solid shell of iron nuclei, under a thin, hot atmosphere just centimeters thick.

files: Chandra X-ray Observations of the Crab Nebula (2011-crab-more-2 - 154).jpg
visual.query: Chandra X-ray Observations of the Crab Nebula (2011-crab-more-2 - 154)

segments.headline: An iron crust

segments.text: Deeper down, the nuclei may be squeezed into strange shapes, like spaghetti and lasagna sheets. Physicists really call it nuclear pasta.

files: Vela Supernova Remnant - Noirlab2406a.jpg
visual.query: Vela Supernova Remnant - Noirlab2406a

segments.headline: Nuclear pasta

segments.text: Computer models suggest nuclear pasta could be the strongest material in the universe, about ten billion times stronger than steel.
And at the very center? Maybe a soup of neutrons. Maybe something even stranger, made of quarks, the building blocks inside protons and neutrons. It's one of the great open questions in physics.

files: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept.jpg
visual.query: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept

segments.headline: The deepest mystery

segments.text: To find out, an instrument on the International Space Station called NICER watches neutron stars in X-rays, measuring their size and weight very precisely.

files: Good Morning From the International Space Station.jpg
visual.query: Good Morning From the International Space Station

segments.headline: NICER on the ISS

segments.text: Sometimes the crust cracks under the strain. These starquakes can make a pulsar suddenly change its spin, a little glitch in its cosmic clock.

files: Moving heart of the Crab Nebula.jpg
visual.query: Moving heart of the Crab Nebula

segments.headline: Starquakes

segments.text: And there's a limit. If a neutron star gains too much mass, around two to three times our Sun, nothing can hold it up anymore. It collapses into a black hole.

visual.label: the limit before a black hole

segments.text: Many neutron stars spin incredibly fast. When a star collapses, it spins faster, like an ice skater pulling in her arms.

files: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept.jpg
visual.query: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept

segments.headline: Spinning faster

segments.text: Some sweep beams of radio waves across space, like a lighthouse. Each time the beam passes Earth, we see a pulse. We call them pulsars.

files: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept.jpg
visual.query: PIA21085 - Pulsar Artist's Concept

segments.headline: Pulsars

segments.text: In nineteen sixty-seven, a young astronomer named Jocelyn Bell Burnell noticed a strange, perfectly regular signal. It was so regular that her team jokingly labeled it L G M one: little green men.

files: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way).jpg
visual.query: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way)

segments.headline: Little green men?

segments.text: It wasn't aliens. It was the first pulsar ever found. A spinning dead star.

files: Moving heart of the Crab Nebula.jpg
visual.query: Moving heart of the Crab Nebula

segments.text: The fastest pulsar known spins seven hundred sixteen times every second. Its surface moves at about a quarter of the speed of light.
Pulsars keep time almost as well as atomic clocks. Scientists use them to search for ripples in space itself. And some even have planets, worlds bathed in deadly radiation.

files: Artist's impression of pulsar planet B1620-26c.jpg
visual.query: Artist's impression of pulsar planet B1620-26c

segments.headline: Pulsar planets

segments.text: But the most terrifying neutron stars are called magnetars.

files: Magnetar (artist’s impression) (heic2504a).jpg
visual.query: Magnetar (artist’s impression) (heic2504a)

segments.headline: Magnetars

segments.text: Their magnetic fields can be about a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's. The strongest magnets in the universe.
From halfway to the Moon, a magnetar would wipe every credit card on Earth. And from about a thousand kilometers away, its field would pull apart the atoms in your body.

files: Artist’s impression of the magnetar in the star cluster Westerlund 1.jpg
visual.query: Artist’s impression of the magnetar in the star cluster Westerlund 1

segments.headline: It pulls atoms apart

segments.text: In two thousand four, a magnetar about fifty thousand light-years away released a giant flare. It was so powerful that it disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere, from the other side of the galaxy.

files: Magnetar (artist’s impression) (heic2504a).jpg
visual.query: Magnetar (artist’s impression) (heic2504a)

segments.headline: A flare felt on Earth

segments.text: Here's my second question. If you had to visit one, from a very safe distance: a pulsar, or a magnetar? Tell us which one, and why.

visual.q: Pulsar or magnetar: which would you visit, from a safe distance?

segments.text: And sometimes, two neutron stars orbit each other. Slowly, over millions of years, they spiral closer.

files: Eso1733s Artist's impression of merging neutron stars.jpg
visual.query: Eso1733s Artist's impression of merging neutron stars

segments.headline: A deadly dance

segments.text: In the final seconds, they whirl around each other hundreds of times a second, and crash.

files: Eso1733s Artist's impression of merging neutron stars.jpg
visual.query: Eso1733s Artist's impression of merging neutron stars

segments.text: On August seventeenth, twenty seventeen, detectors on Earth felt the ripples in space from one of these crashes, a hundred thirty million light-years away. Then telescopes around the world saw the flash.

files: Artist's impression of a kilonova explosion.jpg
visual.query: Artist's impression of a kilonova explosion

segments.headline: August 17, 2017

segments.text: The explosion, called a kilonova, forged heavy elements: gold, platinum, and more. Enough to outweigh Earth many times over.

files: Artist's impression of a kilonova explosion.jpg
visual.query: Artist's impression of a kilonova explosion

segments.headline: A gold factory

segments.text: Much of the gold on Earth was probably made this way, long before our solar system was born. The gold in a ring or a necklace may have come from neutron stars colliding.

files: Earth's City Lights by DMSP, 1994-1995 (large).jpg
visual.query: Earth's City Lights by DMSP, 1994-1995 (large)

segments.headline: The gold in your jewelry

segments.text: How many neutron stars are out there? Astronomers think our galaxy may hold around a hundred million of them. Most are old, cold and dark, and we'll never see them.

files: Center of the Milky Way Galaxy IV – Composite.jpg
visual.query: Center of the Milky Way Galaxy IV – Composite

segments.headline: About 100 million

segments.text: So far, we've found more than three thousand pulsars, mostly with radio telescopes.
What if one wandered into our solar system? Even passing far beyond Neptune, its gravity could scramble the orbits of the planets. Thankfully, no known neutron star is headed our way.

files: The Solar System Montage - GPN-2000-000454.jpg
visual.query: The Solar System Montage - GPN-2000-000454

segments.headline: A wandering dead star?

segments.text: So, would you ever want to meet a neutron star? Not up close. The radiation, the gravity, and the magnetism would each destroy you long before you reached it.

files: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron).jpg
visual.query: Artist's Illustration of Neutron Star (2009-cassio-more-2 - neutron)

segments.headline: The verdict

segments.text: But from far away, they are some of the most useful objects in the universe. They test Einstein's theories, keep cosmic time, and they made some of the atoms around you.

files: Vela Supernova Remnant - Noirlab2406a.jpg
visual.query: Vela Supernova Remnant - Noirlab2406a

segments.text: Every time you see something golden, remember. It might be a souvenir from two dead stars.

visual.query: Tycho-supernova-xray
